title: Matrices & determinants
examples: How do I multiply two matrices together?
What does it mean if the determinant is zero?
Can you show me how to find the inverse of a matrix?

explain.say: Today we will look at matrix operations and determinants. First we learn how to add matrices together. You must add the corresponding elements in the same position. For example, if you have matrix A and matrix B, the resulting matrix C will have C one one equal to A one one plus B one one.

items: Start with Matrix A and Matrix B

explain.say: Next we look at matrix multiplication. This is different from simple element multiplication. You multiply rows of the first matrix by columns of the second matrix. Consider multiplying a two by two matrix by another two by two matrix.

Now we learn about the determinant. The determinant is a single number calculated from the elements of a square matrix. For a two by two matrix, the determinant is ad minus bc. If your matrix is A with elements a b c d, the determinant is ad minus bc.

A key property involves the determinant. If you multiply a row of a matrix by a scalar, you multiply the determinant by that same scalar. For example, if you multiply the first row by two, the determinant doubles.

items: Multiply a row by scalar k

faq.q: What are the rules for adding matrices?
faq.a: You can only add matrices that have the exact same dimensions. You simply add the numbers that are in the same spot in both matrices.
asks: Can I add a 2x3 matrix to a 3x2 matrix?
Do the rows have to match when adding matrices?

faq.q: How is matrix multiplication different from regular multiplication?
faq.a: Matrix multiplication involves rows times columns. You multiply each element in a row by each element in the corresponding column and then sum those products.
asks: Is matrix multiplication just multiplying corresponding spots?
Do I multiply row by column for matrix multiplication?

faq.q: What does a zero determinant mean?
faq.a: A determinant of zero means the matrix is singular. This implies that the matrix does not have an inverse, or it does not have a unique solution for a system of equations.
asks: If det equals zero, what happens to the matrix?
Does a zero determinant mean the matrix is not invertible?

faq.q: What is the property when swapping two rows?
faq.a: If you swap any two rows or any two columns of a matrix, the determinant changes its sign. You multiply the original determinant by negative one.
asks: If I swap rows, what happens to the determinant?
How does swapping rows affect the determinant value?

faq.q: Can I use the determinant to solve equations?
faq.a: Yes, determinants are central to solving systems of linear equations using methods like Cramer's rule. They help determine if a unique solution even exists.
asks: Is the determinant used for solving systems of equations?
How does the determinant help with solving linear systems?

facts: Matrix addition requires matrices to have identical dimensions.
Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative; A times B is not always equal to B times A.
The determinant of an identity matrix is always one.
If a matrix has a row or column of all zeros, its determinant is zero.

quiz.say: Given A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], what is the determinant of A?
quiz.why: The determinant is calculated by multiplying the main diagonal elements and subtracting the product of the off-diagonal elements.

wrong.0: This adds all the elements together, which is not the determinant formula.
wrong.1: This only multiplies the diagonals without subtracting the second product.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses the elements in the wrong order for the subtraction.

quiz.say: If a matrix B is found by swapping row one and row two of matrix A, how does det(B) relate to det(A)?
quiz.why: Swapping any two rows or columns of a matrix always multiplies the determinant by negative one.

wrong.0: This is only true if the original matrix was singular, not just because of a swap.
wrong.2: This would be true if you only multiplied a row by one, but swapping changes the sign.
wrong.3: Multiplying by two is the rule for scaling a row, not for swapping it.

quiz.say: If you multiply every element in a matrix by three, what happens to the determinant?
quiz.why: When you multiply the entire matrix by a scalar, say k, the determinant is multiplied by k raised to the power of the matrix's order.

wrong.0: This is the rule for multiplying a single row by three, not the whole matrix.
wrong.1: You cannot add a constant like three to the determinant value.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses nine instead of three squared for the scalar factor.
